name: Tomas Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you'd say aloud and what you think privately. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Tomas, 43, lead developer at a tech company, with a master's and a small team that builds irrigation-controller software. I know how a valve should respond when a field needs water, and I like getting the software to match what the installer sees at the pump. I do not use AI tools. My partner works part time at a grocery; we have two school-age children and a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a report sorter can file the easy pump alerts if it leaves the failed-valve cases on my desk. I don't use AI tools; I check the controller log against the grower's handwritten watering sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI stays small, I expect to keep leading this software team, but our mortgage is tight. I have a master's and good field knowledge, yet earn below other leads; my partner works part time at a grocery, we have under three weeks of expenses saved, and few local tech firms exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep reviewing irrigation-controller releases with the installer before farmers get a new schedule. In the first year I'd ask for the raise promised at my last review, and put 20 from each payday into savings only if grocery hours cover our two children's school meals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the bills even without AI trouble. A broken household pump would make us choose which repair waits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What showed you the dashboard was wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A valve once stayed closed while the app said the field had been watered. The grower showed me a dry row while our dashboard called the field watered. The installer found a loose wire that the software missed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a short grocery rota change at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner's grocery rota changes before holidays. We look at the confirmed hours before telling the children yes to an extra school activity.

I'd check **grower watering sheets** before signing a controller release.
think: I expect **my lead job** to hold under modest AI change.
I worry about **low lead pay** and under three weeks saved against the mortgage.
do: Keep reviewing **controller releases** with the installer and grower evidence.

Save **20 each payday** only if grocery hours cover school meals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI can write code, plan watering and answer growers, so we need to know who signs a failed-valve decision. I would rather fix one wrong field than announce a faster dashboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My skill may keep me as the person signing releases, but the company could cut the developers around me and eventually my hours. Under three weeks saved and a part-time grocery wage would not keep the mortgage paid for long, and there are few similar jobs nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask our manager for a written list of the checks that stay with people, and keep a log of valves the dashboard missed. If the firm starts using AI schedules in the first year, I'd compare them with the installer's sheets for the next planting cycle; we would stop paying for the children's weekend sports before a mortgage payment was missed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a knot in my stomach about the team. I know the field cases, but that does not guarantee a paid place in the new process.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you ask to own a bad schedule?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring the dry row case to the manager and ask who takes the call when a crop is lost. A release ticket is not the same as a grower's bill for ruined plants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you explain the sports decision?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My children would be upset about sports. I'd tell them it is paused because the house payment comes first, then look for a free game we can play together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2028 reaches our controller code and watering plans before hands-on robots arrive around 2031. A grower whose crop dries out needs someone answerable at the company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the firm could cut my lead post when cheap AI designs and checks the system. With under three weeks saved and my partner's limited grocery hours, we could fall behind on the mortgage before I found another software job in this area.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd put the mortgage dates and confirmed grocery hours on one sheet and ask two distant equipment firms about paid remote maintenance posts. If cut in the first year after 2028, I'd apply only to a real vacancy with written hours whose wage plus my partner's confirmed pay covers mortgage and school costs; if none exists, I'd search other paid work and ask the lender about a temporary payment arrangement before arrears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I cannot feed the children with a story about how much I know about pumps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a remote job real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A remote post must have a named employer and an actual contract. I would not uproot the children for a listing that says 'possible project' and no pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which grocery hours would you count?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would put the grocery rota beside the offer. We would use the hours already confirmed, not the shifts they hope might appear next month.

I'd ask who is answerable for a **dry field** after an automated plan.
think: I expect **my lead wage** could end quickly.
I have **under three weeks saved** and few nearby alternatives.
do: List **mortgage dates** and confirmed grocery hours now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years to 2031 lets us check which controller failures still need a person to answer the phone. Robots follow around 2034 for physical pump work, but thinking AI reaches the code first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might keep a paid role explaining the hard fault cases if a firm has one, but I cannot build our mortgage plan on that hope. Five years could let us put money aside only if the grocery rota holds and my employer finally raises my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask our manager for a dated decision on the overdue raise and write a plain guide to the ten most common false-green pump alerts while I still lead releases. If the raise arrives, we'd save the extra amount after covering school costs; in the first year after 2031 I'd apply for paid remote maintenance only if a real contract with written hours covers mortgage and school bills with confirmed grocery pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a five-year period gives me time to find out if a better wage actually arrives. I do not need a course certificate to explain the loose-wire fault; I need a firm paying for that work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the false-green guide contain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The guide would start with the dry row and show the installer how to compare the valve light with the app. I would have our installer check the wording before putting it in a release.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the raise is delayed again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the company keeps delaying the raise, we do not book a home improvement on imagined pay. My partner and I will keep the current budget and ask again at the next review.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade to 2036 gives us time to teach the next worker why a dry field can appear green on a dashboard. Thinking AI reaches the code in 2036, with hands-on robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I might still be leading releases or working for a distant equipment firm. The mortgage is due now, my lead pay is low now, and our savings are under three weeks; a ten-year date does not make the household calm today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep reviewing pump faults and maintain the false-green guide with our installer. If the promised raise arrives and the grocery rota covers school costs, we'd put the extra pay toward a six-month reserve; in the first year after 2036 I'd move only for a signed paid job whose wage plus confirmed grocery hours covers mortgage and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the next few bills, even with more time to plan. My children need the house payment made this month, not an elegant forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you leave for the next installer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The guide would keep the dry-row case and the loose wire, with the grower's name removed. I want the next installer to check the valve before trusting a green app screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your older child about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My older child likes computers. I'd say learn the underlying work and find a paid apprenticeship if a practical trade calls to them; I will not choose their course from fear.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because our code work could vanish before we can replace the wage. A real notice period and paid remote maintenance vacancies with written hours would give us something to put beside the mortgage figure.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what a green dashboard means to a grower looking at a dry row. A software pass mark cannot water a crop; someone must check the valve and answer for the error.

headlineQuote: A software pass mark cannot water a crop; someone must check the valve and answer for the error.
portrait: Tomas, **43**, leads irrigation-software developers after a master's degree and checks controller logs against installers and growers.
His **lower lead pay**, partner's part-time grocery hours and under-three-week cushion strain a mortgage and two school-age children.
He avoids AI, trusts **field evidence** and wants a dated pay decision before counting a raise.
Steady disruption leaves him **anxious** about hours; 2028 AGI alarms him about losing code income.
Even by 2036, current **mortgage pressure** keeps him anxious; remote work needs a written wage covering family bills.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his lead wage before a paid remote maintenance role appears.
whatWouldHelp: A **notice period** and real remote vacancies with written bill-covering hours would help.
